query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled aging heat treatment to induce fine, coherent Ni3Ti precipitates in a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy treated only by solution processing.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are primary constituents, processed via arc melting and homogenized by solution treatment resulting in a single-phase, homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: After solution treatment, subject the alloy to an aging heat treatment (for example, at 700°C for 4 hours) followed by rapid quenching to precipitate nanoscale Ni3Ti intermetallic particles.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical tests performed at ~700°C in an inert atmosphere; tests may include low strain rate creep measurements and yield strength evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, coherent Ni3Ti precipitates within the primary matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: the coherent Ni3Ti particles hinder dislocation motion at high temperatures, delaying creep deformation and increasing yield strength relative to a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in yield strength and/or enhanced creep resistance at elevated temperatures (700°C) compared to the baseline solution-treated alloy.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy processed only by solution treatment, which lacks the strengthening precipitates.
generation.boundary: The aging treatment is expected to be effective within a temperature range around 700°C and aging times of roughly 1–10 hours; outside of these processing limits, precipitate formation may be inefficient or lead to detrimental particle coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of mechanical property enhancement is uncertain due to variability in precipitate distribution and kinetics of precipitation; optimal aging parameters may require further refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy: one set receives only the solution treatment (baseline), and the other is subjected to the additional aging step (700°C for 4 hours, then quenched). Perform elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., yield strength and creep tests at 700°C) and carry out microstructural characterization (TEM and XRD) to assess the presence and distribution of Ni3Ti precipitates.
measurements: Precipitate size and density via transmission electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in yield strength or creep resistance, or if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the formation of fine, coherent Ni3Ti precipitates compared to the solution-treated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
